title: Norway’s Telenor telecom faces lawsuit for giving user data to Myanmar junta
content:
The state-owned company is accused of abetting crimes against humanity

Originally published on Global Voices

Telenor telecom operated in Myanmar from 2014 to 2022. Photo by Bjoertvedt. Source: Wikipedia. CC BY-SA 4.0

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The Norway-based multinational telecom company Telenor is facing charges for its role in turning over sensitive customer data to the military government of Myanmar.

If successful, the case would be the first ever to hold a telecom company accountable for failing to protect user data from being misused by an authoritarian regime.
snippet:
The state-owned company is accused of abetting crimes against humanity

title: In Kyrgyzstan, persons with disabilities are collecting proof of physical barriers to hold the government accountable
content:
Physical barriers are being exposed by those who are affected the most

Originally published on Global Voices

Participants of the Oasis Data Lab workshop in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. Image by the public fund Oasis. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Kyrgyzstan’s progress in creating an inclusive and accessible environment for people with disabilities remains limited after seven years of ratifying the United Nations (UN) Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2019.

Despite a legal responsibility to undertake measures that would remove legal and physical barriers and help people with disabilities lead independent social and economic lives, the government has not prioritized this commitment at the level requested by the country’s disabled community.
snippet:
Physical barriers are being exposed by those who are affected the most

title: After flood disasters, Nepal needs clear numbers on aid and a reconstruction plan
content:
Nepali communities live in the shadow of natural hazards, where uncertainty and fear are daily realities

Originally published on Global Voices

Settlements across the Tadi River, Devighat in Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal on October 7, 2026. Used with permission.

Forty-six days later, just when Nepal was trying to recover from the Bhotekoshi flash flood, which struck the Nepal–Tibet border regions, affecting Rasuwa and Nuwakot, another landslide-induced flood hit Chumnubri, Gorkha, on October 11, 2026. This latest disaster has added to the wounds of communities who live in the shadow of natural hazards, where uncertainty and fear are daily realities.

The climate-related disaster in Nuwakot has devastated a once-popular tourist landscape, destroying its natural beauty and economic opportunities, with settlements heartbreakingly reduced to rubble and vital infrastructure, including roads, bridges and hydro-power facilities, washed away. The full death toll remains officially unconfirmed.

Survivors still come to search for their belongings in Devighatm, Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal on October 7, 2026. Used with permission.
snippet:
Nepali communities live in the shadow of natural hazards, where uncertainty and fear are daily realities

title: Poetry book promotes Chabacano, Asia’s only Spanish-based creole language
content:
Ten authors and 23 poems are featured in the anthology

Originally published on Global Voices

Photo from the Facebook page of Voces del Alma. Used with permission

A new poetry anthology features writers of Chabacano, one of the Philippines’ 170 languages, which is widely spoken in the southernmost city of Zamboanga, and stands out as Asia’s only Spanish-based creole language.

The Philippines was a colony of Spain for more than three centuries, but the Spanish language was only used by the elite, friars, and colonial rulers. Only in Zamboanga did a Spanish-based creole language develop.

In 2018, Global Voices featured Bien Chabacano, a blog dedicated to promoting and documenting Chavacano de Zamboanga. Its creator, Jerome Herrera, launched a book project this year by inviting writers to submit poems to be compiled in an anthology. This led to the launch of the “Sombra y Luz” book in July, featuring 23 poems by 10 authors. The poems are mainly about love, family, and Zamboangueño identity.

title: What African elections can learn from the Borana Gadaa system
content:
Can the Borana Gadaa system inspire fairer elections, peaceful transitions, and stronger democracy across Africa?

Originally published on Global Voices

A Balli Walirafudhu handover ceremony held by the Borana Oromo people in Southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya. They have long practiced rotational, peaceful leadership transfer, known as the Borana Gadaa system. Photo used with permission.

This article by Diba Kosi Bilinga was originally published by Peace News Network on July 20, 2026. An edited version is being republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement.

Every election season, much of Africa braces itself. In some cases, incumbents amend constitutions to erase term limits, and citizens wait to see whether power will change hands at the ballot box or in the streets. The pattern repeats: disputed results, ethnic mobilization, coups, or leaders who refuse to leave.
snippet:
Can the Borana Gadaa system inspire fairer elections, peaceful transitions, and stronger democracy across Africa?

title: Bangladesh-Malaysia recruitment reforms revive old questions over the cost of migration
content:
Repeated disruptions raise concerns over recruitment transparency and migrant workers’ protection from exploitation.

Originally published on Global Voices

On Saturday, October 5, 2024, a Memorandum of Collaboration (MOC) was signed in Dhaka between the Wage Earners Welfare Board and Malaysia's PERKESO, regarding the expansion of the labor market in Malaysia. Image via Wikipedia by Press Information Department of Bangladesh. Public Domain.

Officials in both Bangladesh and Malaysia’s have made repeated attempts to reform the countries’ labour migration relationship, leading to numerous suspensions and reopenings over more than three decades.

However, on August 30, 2026, Bangladesh’s State Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives, Mir Shahe Alam, announced that Malaysia would recruit around 200,000 Bangladeshi workers over six months, with departures expected to begin in late September. He also referred to a plan to send 10,000 workers without requiring them to bear migration costs.
snippet:
Repeated disruptions raise concerns over recruitment transparency and migrant workers’ protection from exploitation.

title: When free speech has a price: Youth voices in Mozambique
content:
When speaking freely can have a cost, young people turn to music to challenge political silence

Originally published on Global Voices

A group of men during a peaceful protest; one of them holds a microphone and a banner. Photo taken by Stephanie Douglas. Nigeria. Via Pexels. Pexels License.

In Mozambique, freedom of expression is regulated by the Law on the Right to Information No. 34/2014, a constitutionally guaranteed right under Article 48 of the Constitution of the Republic of Mozambique. However, for many young people, speaking publicly about corruption, inequality, police violence, or accountability continues to carry risk, showing the gap between the promises of democracy and actual daily experience.

When speaking freely can have a cost, young people turn to music to challenge political silence

title: How Ecuador is fighting to keep industrial trans fats off the food shelf
content:
A public health battle over what ends up on Ecuador’s food shelves

Originally published on Global Voices

Civil society, academia, and the State met in Quito to discuss progress toward the regulation of trans fatty acids in a country where non-communicable diseases account for more than 76% of deaths. Photo by Salomé Rosales Estrella/Minga por la Pachamama, 2026. Used with permission.

“What are we eating? Foods that regenerate or products that degenerate life?” asked Eliana Estrella on September 7, 2026, in the auditorium of Universidad San Francisco de Quito in Ecuador. The popular communicator and member of the Committee of Users of the Food Market (CUUM) was speaking at the Hearts Free of Trans Fats meeting, before social organizations, academia and health agencies.

title: Trump’s ‘Agreements on Reciprocal Trade’ (ARTs) threaten equitable access to the internet in Global South
content:
The provision could give the U.S. the power to exclude Chinese ICT suppliers in signatory countries

Originally published on Global Voices

Image remix on Canva by Ihsan Kamil/EngageMedia. Used with permission.

This article, written by Prapasiri “Nan” Suttisome, was first published by EngageMedia, a non-profit media, technology, and culture organization, and an edited version is republished here as part of a content-sharing agreement. It is also part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

Around the world, one in every three people has no reliable access to the internet. Unequal access to the internet creates digital divides that can limit civic participation, undermine access to education and healthcare, and deepen inequality. It can also reduce innovation, industrial growth, and economic output. Reducing digital divides is recognized as essential for progress on the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals, as reaffirmed by the more recent Global Digital Compact, 2024.

title: Subsea cables and oil pipelines: The infrastructure linking AI, empire, and occupation
content:
Internet infrastructure policy is increasingly a topic of discussion in military strategy and policy decision-making

Originally published on Global Voices

Screenshot of the Internet Infrastructure Map in 2026, from kmcd.dev. Fair use

By Alli Armijo

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The internet has always been illusive. Stretching bodies of water, screens, and time zones, it exists in a plurality increasingly shaped by big tech. And the cables mediate this; the cables are its nervous system.

With over 600 active and planned underwater internet cables spanning over 1.5 million kilometers around the globe, the majority of subsea infrastructure is predominantly owned and operated by US tech monopolies, namely Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft. 

This infrastructure is largely laid on trans-Atlantic slave ship and oil extraction routes, algorithmically bound by a legacy of colonial violence and exploitative labor practices.
snippet:
Internet infrastructure policy is increasingly a topic of discussion in military strategy and policy decision-making

title: Alibaba sues Pentagon to denounce being classified as a Chinese military affiliate
content:
China’s big tech governance model looms over Alibaba’s lawsuit against the Pentagon

Originally published on Global Voices

Image created by Oiwan Lam with Canva.

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

As the U.S. Department of Defense expanded its Section 1260H list of “Chinese military companies operating in the U.S.” in June 2026, three dominant internet and technology giants — Baidu, Alibaba and Tencent (BAT) — have been flagged as an extension of the Chinese state and subject to the Pentagon procurement ban that excludes them from DoD’s supply chain. The listing also signals an increasing risk of further sanctions from the Department of Commerce or the Treasury.

title: El Niño speeds climate crisis and tests Latin America’s food security
content:
As the climate pattern intensifies, Latin America faces a growing food security challenge

Originally published on Global Voices

Illustration made by Connectas. Used with permission.

This article by Fabiola Chambi first appeared in CONNECTAS, in Spanish, on September 2, 2026. An edited version is being republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement.

“We are sad, completely desperate. We have lost llamas, alpacas, sheep — we haven’t even been able to count them all yet […] That is how we make a living. We put our children through school and sell our products in the city.” The last heavy snowfall René Luna could remember had caught him by surprise nearly 25 years ago, but never anything like this. A blanket of snow covered the landscape, and hundreds of animals were buried in his municipality in central Bolivia, which has now been declared a disaster zone.
snippet:
As the climate pattern intensifies, Latin America faces a growing food security challenge

title: Africa’s governments already treat the internet as protest infrastructure. Its courts have not caught up
content:
When many people gather, some states are not prosecuting people. Instead, it cuts the network

Originally published on Global Voices

Kenya Judiciary building.  Image by Wing via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

This piece is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

On a Saturday in late July 2025, Angola shut down its internet for the first time in its recorded history. Not during an election, and not during a war. People had taken to the streets to protest the rising price of fuel. At least 22 people were killed according to the authorities’ own figures; civil society monitors counted 30 dead and more than 1,500 arrested.
snippet:
When many people gather, some states are not prosecuting people. Instead, it cuts the network

title: Digital hopes, real power: From connection to collective action
content:
Understanding how the digital rights movement evolved requires a closer look at the communities that shaped it

Originally published on Global Voices

Tahrir Square, Cairo, Egypt, February 8, 2011. Photo by Mona on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0).

This article was originally published by the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) on April 30, 2026, and an edited version is republished here with permission. It is also part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

Back in 2011, the term “digital rights” was still fairly new. In the decades prior, open source and hacker communities, as well as a handful of organizations, had advocated for digital freedoms. It was through the merging of disparate communities from around the world in the 2000s that digital rights came to be more clearly understood as an extension of fundamental human rights.

title: Young people are bridging the climate divide for Oceania and the Caribbean
content:
When communities are included, when solutions are discussed, understood, and locally relevant, collaboration and participation follow

Originally published on Global Voices

Maps of Oceania and the Caribbean superimposed over the image of a young person looking at a storm brewing on the horizon. Feature image created by Janine Mendes-Franco using Canva Pro elements.

By Adele Roeder, Orit Novak, Chelsea Adams and Zahiris P. Francisco

This article was originally published by Future Forward Australia on May 10, 2026. An edited version is published here with permission.

Young people are no strangers to seeing the impacts of climate change. In Australia alone, the catastrophic Black Summer bushfires of 2019–20, record-breaking floods across northern parts of the country in 2026, and most recently, the severe tropical cyclone Narelle, which badly affected three states, have all left their mark.

title: How authoritarian states are building an international market for digital surveillance
content:
The main danger of AI in authoritarian regimes is the ability to suppress any protest

Originally published on Global Voices

Moscow subway cameras are connected to a facial recognition system. Screenshot taken from the YouTube video “Facial recognition cameras help detain dissidents in the Moscow metro” by the DW YouTube channel; fair use.

Sonya, from Stavropol Krai, Russia, is 15 years old. In June 2026, she was sentenced to 70 hours of compulsory labor, connected to a February 2026 incident in which she had written the surname “Navalny” on a bus stop. That stop happened to be in a district that was being monitored by officers from the Center for Combating Extremism, commonly called Center E. Similarly, Yuri, a pensioner from Astrakhan who was also identified from surveillance footage, was given three years of restricted freedom for writing “No to War” in red marker on buildings.
snippet:
The main danger of AI in authoritarian regimes is the ability to suppress any protest
